-104.87500,39.52930.name: Colorado Center for Reproductive Medicine
-104.87500,39.52930.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: William B. Schoolcraft, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

13.34701,52.53973.name: RKI Centre for Biological Threats and Special Pathogens (Zentrum für Biologische Gefahren und Spezielle Pathogene, ZBS)
13.34701,52.53973.company: Robert Koch Institute, Federal Ministry of Health
13.34701,52.53973.desc: A BSL4 laboratory, operational. Run by Robert Koch Institute, Federal Ministry of Health. It is categorised as a public health laboratory, working on human health. Personnel work in full-body positive-pressure suits with their own air supply. Containment space: 330 SqM. Operational or announced: 2018. It stands in a built-up area, with more than fifty thousand people living within two and a half miles. There is no international register of laboratories at this containment level and no obligation to declare one, so this record comes from a research project rather than a regulator. What that project could not find out is absent here too.

-86.15810,39.76840.name: Corteva — CRISPR licensing framework
-86.15810,39.76840.desc: Corteva holds or licenses much of the foundational CRISPR intellectual property for agriculture, and has published terms under which universities and small companies may use it. That sounds like openness and functions as a chokepoint: the terms are set by one party, apply to a technique everyone now needs, and can be revised. Whoever writes the licence decides which agricultural editing gets done, and by whom — more influence over the field’s direction than any single product carries.

-76.98200,39.03500.name: FDA — cellular & gene therapy approvals
-76.98200,39.03500.state: Silver Spring — CBER, 10903 New Hampshire Ave, Bldg 71
-76.98200,39.03500.desc: The US regulator’s list of approved cell and gene therapies, each with its review documents. The files record what the agency asked, what the sponsor answered, and where reviewers disagreed — which makes this the most detailed public account anywhere of how genetic medicines get cleared.

-76.98200,39.03500.name: FDA MedWatch — reporting an adverse event yourself
-76.98200,39.03500.state: Silver Spring, Maryland — FDA, 10903 New Hampshire Avenue
-76.98200,39.03500.desc: A patient, a relative or a carer can file a report directly, without a doctor and without permission. This matters more for gene and cell therapies than for ordinary medicines, because so few people have received any one of them: with a few hundred patients treated worldwide, a single well-described report is a measurable fraction of everything known about that product. The equivalents are the Yellow Card scheme in the UK and EudraVigilance in the EU. Reports are public in aggregate, so it is also where to look before consenting to something.
